title: Belonging
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino opens with a personal reflection on the feeling of belonging she gets from communal singing at Mass, and uses it as the emotional throughline for a practical post about building belonging through classroom participation technique - specifically choral response. She admits an earlier attempt at choral response fizzled because the cueing was inconsistent and slow, and uses that failure to design a clearer version built around a simple stop/go hand gesture, distinct from the countdown cues she already uses for mini-whiteboard questions. She situates the technique within an existing sequence she borrows from Pritesh Raichura - securing attention first through checks for listening, then building in rehearsal time, before finally checking understanding - arguing choral response fits best for content that needs to be simply known and repeated, like naming subcellular structures, rather than deep conceptual material. Her stated aim is modest and specific: choral response alone won't manufacture belonging, but it offers quiet or passive students, particularly in GCSE classes, a genuine and low-risk way to be part of the group's shared answer rather than sitting out of verbal participation entirely.
points: Castelino draws her framework for classroom belonging from an unexpected source - the communal experience of singing at Mass - translating voices joined together into a case for choral response as a participation technique.

She's candid about a prior failed attempt at choral response, diagnosing the failure as procedural (clunky cues, inconsistent routine) rather than conceptual, and uses that diagnosis to redesign the technique with clearer hand signals.

Her sequencing - attention, then rehearsal, then check for understanding - borrows explicitly from Pritesh Raichura's checks for listening, positioning choral response as the next rung on an existing participation ladder rather than a standalone gimmick.

Castelino frames the technique's value narrowly and honestly: it won't build belonging on its own, but it gives quiet, GCSE-level passive students a low-risk way to physically participate alongside the class.
quotes: It got me thinking about my students and helping them to feel belonging in my classroom. Giving every student the chance to speak, to rehearse and to join in together can be a powerful way to help them feel they belong.

I must confess, I have tried choral response before and it hasn’t worked very well. Because it is not a standard technique in my classroom, the instructions and the cue always seemed clunky and it took several minutes to get students to give me a one-word answer to a question.

I want my students to feel the same way about learning in the classroom. I want them to feel at home and know that they are safe to respond to quick questions as a class. I want them to feel like we are all in this together.
As with Mass yesterday, the first step is attention. My students need to be fully attending to what I am saying and what we are learning about.

This one technique alone will not build belonging in my classroom but it can certainly provide an opportunity for those quiet, less confident students to feel like they are a part of the class, working together to participate.
The reason I am planning to use gestures instead of a countdown is because it is quite different to the other cues I use such as 1..2...3...Show when posing questions for mini-whiteboards.
